responsibility: `rustc_ast` defines and exposes the compiler’s parsed Rust abstract syntax tree layer: the canonical in-memory representation of source code, its tokens, attributes, and traversal/manipulation interfaces that the parser, macro expansion, early analysis, and lowering stages share before HIR. Its crate root (`lib.rs`) assembles this API, re-exports the core pieces, organizes the major modules, and provides the stable-hashing hook needed for AST participation in compiler hashing. The core syntax model lives in `ast.rs`, which declares the principal AST node types for items, expressions, patterns, types, statements, generics, paths, literals, functions, traits, impls, foreign items, and related metadata. `ast_traits.rs` adds uniform traits over those heterogeneous nodes so compiler code can access common capabilities such as node IDs, attributes, token streams, and pointer-like wrappers generically. `node_id.rs` supplies the `NodeId` identity space and associated map/set support used to index AST nodes before later lowering assigns downstream identifiers, while `ptr.rs` provides the pervasive `P<T>` ownership abstraction used to store and rewrite AST nodes efficiently. For the lexical and token-preserving side of parsed syntax, `token.rs` defines the token vocabulary, delimiters, literals, comments, macro metavariable/nonterminal categories, interpolated fragments, and related classification and hashing behavior, and `tokenstream.rs` builds the persistent token-tree/token-stream representation, including delimiter and spacing metadata, lazy and attribute-aware streams, iteration APIs, and token-to-attribute desugaring support. The `attr` module is the AST-layer attribute subsystem: it represents attributes and meta items, allocates attribute IDs, parses attribute tokens into structured forms and literals, constructs common attribute and doc-comment nodes, and offers query/search helpers over attribute collections. The `util` module provides shared low-level AST support for parser and syntax interpretation needs, including parser-oriented precedence and syntactic-classification helpers, literal conversion/validation and unescaping, comment classification and doc-text normalization, and Unicode scanning for text-flow control characters. For traversing and transforming syntax trees, `visit.rs` defines the standard read-only `Visitor` framework and default walks over all major AST shapes, while `mut_visit.rs` provides the mutable traversal and in-place rewrite framework with flat-map helpers, token-aware mutation support, and dummy-node utilities for structural rewriting. `entry.rs` classifies parsed functions and items as crate entry points such as `main`, `#[start]`, `#[rustc_main]`, nested `main`, or non-entry functions so later stages can handle startup semantics and diagnostics consistently. The `expand` module contributes AST-level expansion support shared with macro expansion and downstream passes, including the representation of items stripped by `cfg` evaluation and the allocator-shim specification used to name, validate, and reason about allocator-related generated items. Together, these modules make `rustc_ast` the compiler crate responsible for representing parsed Rust source faithfully—including both tree and token forms—plus the common metadata, utilities, and visitor infrastructure needed to inspect, classify, hash, and transform that syntax before semantic lowering.
